title: A Tiny Robot That Swims With Living Muscles
summary:
Imagine a robot powered not by batteries and motors, but by living muscle. Scientists at MIT have built exactly that: a tiny swimming robot that flaps its fins using a layer of real muscle cells.

The robot's body is a flexible gel frame about the size of a stick of gum. It has two fins, and each fin is coated with muscle cells far thinner than a human hair. The cells were genetically modified so that they squeeze tight when light shines on them. By flashing light onto one fin or the other, and changing how often the light pulses, the researchers can steer the robot and control its speed. In tests, the paper-thin robot swam and turned through a simple underwater maze. At top speed it covered about four times its own body length every minute. An Olympic swimmer manages up to 65 body lengths per minute, and the little robot's pace is similar to a cow shark cruising lazily through the ocean.

"It takes a lot of force to move through water versus air," said study author Ritu Raman, an associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT. "The robot's quite strong, given its size." The study, published in the journal Advanced Functional Materials, is the first demonstration of a very thin, flat robot that can travel from place to place using living muscle tissue. Most earlier biohybrid robots were built from bulky chunks of lab-grown muscle needing millions of cells. The MIT team believes thinner designs could be cheaper to build and move more efficiently. One day, Raman says, robots powered by living muscle might do delicate jobs in fragile places where ordinary machines are too rough, because living tissue is soft, responds to its surroundings, and can even heal itself.
why_it_matters: Robots driven by living tissue could work gently in fragile places that hard machines might damage, opening a new way to explore and help in delicate environments. The work also suggests that thinner, simpler designs may make such biohybrid robots cheaper to build and more efficient.

background_read: Biohybrid robots are machines that combine living cells with built materials, so real tissue does part of the work instead of a motor.
Muscle moves by squeezing tight, so even a thin layer of muscle cells can flap a soft fin and push a small robot through water.
Scientists can change muscle cells so they react to light, and flashing light on one side or the other becomes a simple way to steer.
Because living tissue is soft, senses its surroundings and can heal itself, such robots could one day handle delicate jobs in fragile places where ordinary machines are too rough.
